dashboard.label: Feed administration
dashboard.description: Upload and import offline vulnerability databases. This app never reaches the network itself.

div.p: This app makes no outbound network requests: it runs on a search head with no route to the internet. Vulnerability data gets in one way - build a bundle on a connected machine, carry it across, import it here.
div.h4: 1. Build a bundle (on a connected machine)
div.pre:
riskability-feed sources # what can be fetched
riskability-feed build --out riskability-feed.tar.gz \ --ecosystem Ubuntu --ecosystem Debian --ecosystem Alpine \ --ecosystem npm --ecosystem PyPI --ecosystem Go --ecosystem Maven \ --kev --epss
div.p: Only the sources you name are downloaded. Pick the distributions and language ecosystems your fleet runs; the Coverage dashboard lists which component types are going unmatched.

Add --cve-list for the CVE encyclopaedia, which is what gives a vulnerability a description and a product name rather than an id and a score. It is the one source that is off by default here and in the wrappers: roughly 600 MB to download and about 120 MB in the bundle you carry, which is a decision worth making deliberately. Without it the encyclopaedia still works and still describes almost every CVE, from the advisory text; it just cannot name a product for anything CISA has not catalogued.
div.h4: 2. Get it onto this search head
div.p: Use the staging directory shown above for large files: nothing has to fit in memory. The upload control is capped at 64 MB because a REST upload is held whole in the search head's memory.
Import replaces the active feed rather than merging into it, so withdrawn advisories and corrected ranges cannot survive. Searches keep seeing the previous feed until the import finishes.
div.h4: Windows estates need one extra source
div.p: Linux packages carry a PURL from the package manager and match against their distribution's own advisories, which makes backport handling possible. Windows has no package manager and no PURL - only a display name and a registry version.
Windows fleets therefore need NVD in the bundle, which carries CPE-keyed ranges:
div.pre: riskability-feed build --out riskability-feed.tar.gz \ --nvd 2015-2026 --mitre --kev --epss \ --ecosystem Ubuntu --ecosystem npm # keep your Linux sources too
div.p: Every Windows finding is reported at low confidence: the component is tied to an advisory through a CPE generated from a display name (“7-Zip 24.08 (x64)” → cpe:2.3:a:igor_pavlov:7-zip:24.08) rather than read a package record. The comparison may be exact while the product identity is a guess: leads to verify, not facts. Installed hotfixes are collected but not yet matched: that needs Microsoft’s MSRC data to ask whether the KB fixing a CVE is installed, a different mechanism from version ranges and not yet implemented.
div.h4: If this search head does have internet access
div.p: Use the Fetch directly panel above. It tests upstream reachability first, so an air-gapped instance fails immediately rather than minutes into a download. No outbound request happens unless you press it: nothing is scheduled, nothing runs at install time.

Feed licences differ: OSV aggregates sources that are individually CC‑BY‑4.0 (GitHub, Red Hat), CC‑BY‑SA‑4.0 (Ubuntu), MIT (AlmaLinux) and BSD (Rocky); CISA KEV is US‑government public domain; EPSS is published by FIRST and expects attribution. Each record keeps its source, so attribution survives into Splunk. Building a bundle for your own organisation is uncontroversial; redistributing one is your decision, which is why nothing ships pre-loaded.
